cultivar: Wuyi cai cha (local small-leaf population bushes)
processing: Fully oxidised, unsmoked Tongmu black, usually from a bud with two leaves just opening (Da Chi Gan takes fully opened leaves): withered, rolled, oxidised and dried at low heat.
harvest_season: Spring, from late April into May, picked after the bud teas; one harvest a year in the reserve.
appearance_dry: Small, tight, slightly curly dark strands with reddish stems and a few bronze tips.
appearance_wet: Small copper leaves with reddish stalks, whole and even.
taste_profile: Honey and dried longan over cocoa and sweet potato, with more body and grip than the bud teas and the same cool, clean Tongmu finish.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan, water near the boil, no rinse, short steeps; the extra leaf makes it forgiving of long steeps. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, usually released from early summer after a short rest; drinks well for two or three years and is often better in its second year. Lao cong (old-bush) Chi Gan is sold with the year and bush age stated.
description:
Xiao Chi Gan is an everyday black tea of Tongmu, the Wuyi village that gave the world Lapsang souchong and Jin Jun Mei. The name means something like 'small red-sweet', and it marks a picking standard rather than a separate tea: usually a bud with two leaves just opening. Da Chi Gan, 'big red-sweet', has the two leaves fully open. The definition comes from sellers rather than a published standard.

The leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised and dried without smoke, just like unsmoked Zheng Shan Xiao Zhong; in practice the names overlap, and Chi Gan is best thought of as the finer-picked end of the unsmoked Tongmu range, below Yin Jun Mei and above standard Xiao Zhong. Some sellers class it as Tong Jun Mei ('copper eyebrow'), which tells you where it sits.

In the cup it is honey and dried longan over cocoa and sweet potato, with a bit more body and grip than the bud teas and that cool, clean finish Tongmu teas share. It is sturdy: water near the boil, no rinse, short steeps, eight or more infusions, and it shrugs off a forgotten steep. Lao cong lots from old bushes add a mossy, woody depth and a longer finish.

It is sold by the current spring harvest, at a fraction of Jin Jun Mei prices. Ask for a named village inside the reserve, since the name is not protected. Check that the leaf is small and even with reddish stalks; big, flat leaf with golden fuzz is from somewhere else.

If you want to understand what 'Tongmu character' means without spending Jin Jun Mei money, this is the tea to buy.
history:
Xiao Chi Gan is a name used by makers around Tongmu in the Wuyi Mountains, and little is documented about it beyond their own usage. It is a picking grade within unsmoked Tongmu black tea rather than a separately recorded tea, and there is no official standard behind it.

Sellers broadly agree on the outline: a bud with two leaves just opening is Xiao Chi Gan, and the same with the two leaves fully open is Da Chi Gan. Some also class it as Tong Jun Mei, the grade below the Jun Mei teas that appeared after 2005. Nobody seems to have recorded when the name first came into use.
